deep.reconstruction:
This page is printed (Fraktur), not a Gauss manuscript. It is p. 61 of an elementary arithmetic textbook, almost certainly Christian Leiste's arithmetic/algebra textbook (Wolfenbüttel, c. 1790), which the bundle name 'HB.Leiste' points to. It covers applications of simple and compound proportion to uniform motion, 'moving force', and carriage charges. The only possible Gauss content is a few faint pencil numbers in the left margin.

Top lines (end of §138). The relation is E·c·t = e·C·T, i.e. E/e = (C·T)/(c·t). Hence C:c = E·t : e·T. If E = e, then C·T = c·t and C:c = t:T (inverse proportion of speed and time for the same effect or distance).

§139, uniform motion (s = v·t).
(1) At the same speed C, distances are as times: S = C·T and r = C·t, so S:r = T:t.
(2) In the same time t, at speeds C and c: r = C·t and s = c·t, so r:s = C:c.
(3) Compounding (1) and (2): S:s = (S/r)(r/s) = (T/t)(C/c), so S:s = CT:ct. Equivalently C:c = (S/T):(s/t).

§140, 'moving force' in the pre-Newtonian sense, i.e. force ∝ mass × velocity imparted (momentum).
(1) Equal speed C: V:K = M:m.
(2) Equal mass m: K:v = C:c.
(3) Compounding: V:v = (V/K)(K/v) = MC:mc. Cross-multiplying gives V·m·c = v·M·C.

§141, carriage charge (Fuhrlohn), compound proportion. Loads are L, l; road lengths S, s; prices P, ρ, p, with roads of equal quality.
(1) Same road S: P:ρ = L:l.
(2) Same load l: ρ:p = S:s.
Compounding: P:p = LS:ls, hence P·l·s = p·L·S.

On the next page the text continues with a road-quality factor, P:q = LSW:lsw. Its worked examples are: x = 20·8·9/(6·15) = 16 hundredweight (Centner), and q = 16·15·4·6/(9·20·3) = 32/3 = 10 2/3 Reichsthaler.

Left-margin pencil numbers (faint; I can read e.g. 572, 1430). These are most plausibly overflow from the computations on the previous page (fractions with denominator 143 = 11·13: 420/572, 120/143, with 572 = 4·143 and 1430 = 10·143). They cannot be reconstructed reliably.
errors: §139.3: the verbal statement 'die Räume [verhalten sich] wie die Producte aus den Geschwindigkeiten' omits 'und den Zeiten'. The formula S:s = CT:ct is correct, but the words are incomplete. This is a slip in the printed textbook.
§140.3: the image reads 'Vmc = vMc'. From V:v = MC:mc it should be V·m·c = v·M·C (capital C). The next page indeed quotes it as Vmc = vMC. This is a printing slip.
§140 uses a pre-Newtonian notion of 'Kraft' (proportional to mass × velocity imparted, i.e. momentum or impulse). This is standard for the period but differs from modern force = mass × acceleration.

results.what: Uniform motion: distances proportional to speed × time, S:s = CT:ct, C:c = S/T : s/t
Moving force proportional to mass × velocity: V:v = MC:mc
Carriage charge proportional to load × distance (× road difficulty): P:p = LS:ls
results.modern_name: compound proportion (Regula de tri composita / rule of five)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a printed elementary textbook (Leiste) containing routine compound-proportion exercises. Gauss's only possible contribution is a few faint, uninterpretable pencil numbers in the margin, apparently continuing arithmetic from the previous page.

transcription_corrections: The page is printed Fraktur text (Leiste textbook), not Gauss's handwriting; only the left-margin pencil numbers are possibly by Gauss.
§140.3 indeed prints 'Vmc = vMc' (lowercase c at the end), which is an error for vMC.
The left-margin pencil numbers are very uncertain; plausible readings include 572 and 1430, consistent with the denominator 143 used on the previous page (120/143, 420/572).
